302.title: The turning
302.hook: the Mevlevi order's turning ceremony, one hand up, one hand down
302.howItsDone: Mevlevi Sufis perform the sama' ceremony with the ney and drum, turning with the right palm up and the left palm down; many other Muslims, including many scholars, do not use music or dance in worship, and Muslims differ on it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, every state a guest: moods that come to teach and then leave, and with hardship, ease. Your line was every state is a guest. Which guest did you greet? Day three hundred two.

Even if you've never been to Turkey, you've probably seen the picture: men in tall honey-colored felt hats and long white skirts, turning, turning, their skirts flaring out like bells, their heads tilted, their eyes half closed. People call them whirling dervishes. It looks like a dance. The people who do it call it something else, and the word they use is about the ears, not the feet. Today, the turning.
screen: `TALL HATS, WHITE SKIRTS.` → `TURNING, EYES HALF CLOSED.` → `A WORD ABOUT THE EARS.`

segments.voice: The word is sama'. It means listening, from the same root as as-Sami', the All-Hearing, one of the names of God we met weeks ago. For Sufis, sama' means listening to music, poetry or the Qur'an with the heart until you're moved by it. The Mevlevi order, named for Rumi, Mawlana, turned that listening into a ceremony. Tradition says Rumi himself would sometimes turn in ecstasy, and people tell a story that it began when he heard goldbeaters hammering in the Konya bazaar. The formal ceremony was shaped after his death, by his son and later generations. Everything in it carries meaning. The tall hat is said to stand for the tombstone of the ego. The white skirt, the shroud. The black cloak they take off at the start, the grave left behind. The music is the ney, the reed flute, and a drum. And the arms: the right palm turned up to the sky, the left palm turned down to the earth. The Mevlevis explain it this way: what comes from God is received through the right hand and passed on to the world through the left. The turner keeps nothing. Receive, give. They turn around their own hearts, and they turn together, like planets. In Turkey, the orders were closed in 1925, and for decades the ceremony survived as a cultural performance. UNESCO now lists it as part of the world's heritage. And Muslims hold different views on music in worship; many scholars do not accept musical sama' at all. We'll come to those differences.
screen: `SAMA' — LISTENING.` · `HAT, SHROUD, CLOAK.` · `RIGHT HAND UP, LEFT HAND DOWN.` · `NOT ALL MUSLIMS ACCEPT IT.` · then, large: `RECEIVE, GIVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: turn slowly once, eyes soft. If you can stand safely, stand. Lift your right hand a little, palm up. Let your left hand hang low, palm down. Let your eyes go soft. Now turn slowly, once, all the way round, feeling the floor under your feet. Then stand still and breathe. If you can't stand, just turn your palms: one up, one down, and sit with them. Picture receiving through one and giving through the other. The bell holds the time.
Sama'. Listening with the heart; for the Mevlevis, the turning ceremony, one hand up, one hand down. Today's word.
Your line: receive, give. Today, when something good comes to you, a kind word, a gift, a bit of luck, pass some of it on before the day ends. Day three hundred two.

screen: `DAY 302 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE TEACHER AND THE CHAIN.`

options: holds on to what was received.
points down, passing it on to the world.
fork.reveal: the left palm faces the earth: what comes from God is passed on. the turner keeps nothing.

original.note: Arabic: listening; in Sufism, listening to music, poetry or the Qur'an with the heart.

trapdoor: what you thought: a spinning dance.
what it means: listening turned into prayer: receive from God with one hand, give to the world with the other.

303.title: The teacher and the chain
303.hook: Sufi orders pass teaching from master to student in chains
303.howItsDone: Members of Sufi orders take a pledge, bay'ah, with a living shaykh and learn the practices of their order's chain; many recite the names of their chain, while many other Muslims learn the faith from scholars and teachers without joining an order.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the turning, sama': listening with the heart, right palm up, left palm down. Your line was receive, give. What did you pass on? Day three hundred three.

Think about how you learned the things that matter most. Not from a book. Your grandmother's recipe that was never written down. The way a coach held your wrist to fix your swing. A trade learned standing next to someone for years. Some knowledge only travels hand to hand. Sufis say the inner path is like that. You can read about it, as al-Ghazali did, but to walk it, most of them say, you need a guide who walked it before you, who learned from someone before them, and so on, back and back. Today, the chain.
screen: `A RECIPE NEVER WRITTEN DOWN.` → `SOME THINGS TRAVEL HAND TO HAND.` → `A GUIDE WHO WALKED IT FIRST.`

segments.voice: The Arabic word is silsilah, a chain, like links of metal. In a Sufi order, every teacher, a shaykh, learned from a teacher, who learned from a teacher, all the way back, the Sufis say, to the Prophet ﷺ himself. Students often memorize the names in their chain, and some recite them. Most Sufi chains pass through 'Ali, the Prophet's cousin and son-in-law. The Naqshbandi order traces its main chain through Abu Bakr. Muslims already knew this shape from the hadith. Every hadith comes with an isnad, a chain of narrators: I heard it from so-and-so, who heard it from so-and-so, who heard the Prophet say. Scholars test every link. The Sufi chain works the same way, but what it passes down isn't only words. It's a way of practice, and what Sufis call blessing. The link is made by a pledge, bay'ah, often with a handclasp between teacher and student. Sufis connect it to a verse in the Qur'an about the companions who pledged themselves to the Prophet. In Pickthall's words: "The Hand of Allah is above their hands." So a chain of hands, one on another, back through the centuries, and above them all, in the Sufis' understanding, God's. There's a warning in the tradition too: a chain is only as good as its links, and Sufi writers themselves warn against false teachers. And many Muslims learn their faith deeply without joining any order. But for those in one, the chain means you never walk alone.
screen: `SILSILAH — A CHAIN.` · `BACK TO THE PROPHET, THROUGH 'ALI OR ABU BAKR.` · `LIKE THE ISNAD OF A HADITH.` · `BAY'AH — THE PLEDGE AND THE HANDCLASP.` · then, large: `A CHAIN OF HANDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank a teacher by name. Sit, and breathe. Think of the people who taught you something that mattered. A parent, a teacher at school, an imam, a coach, a boss, an older friend. Go back one more link if you can: who taught them? Say their names quietly, one by one, like a chain. Then pick one who's still living and decide how you'll thank them today. If you pray, you can pray for every name on your chain. The bell holds the time.
Silsilah. The chain of teachers in a Sufi order, reaching back, hand to hand, toward the Prophet. Today's word.
Your line: a chain of hands. Today, send a thank-you to one person who taught you something, and tell them who you've passed it on to. Day three hundred three.

options: a guide, in a chain of teachers, who walked it before you.

fork.reveal: a shaykh in a silsilah: a teacher who learned from a teacher, back, the Sufis say, to the Prophet.

original.note: Arabic: a chain; in Sufism, the line of teachers from shaykh to student.

what it means: a living line of teachers, hand to hand, passing on a way of practice.
what a scholar hears: silsilah mirrors the hadith isnad; bay'ah is grounded by Sufis in 48:10, the pledge under the tree.

sources.ref: Qur'an 48:10
al-Hujwiri, Kashf al-Mahjub; al-Qushayri, al-Risala (the shaykh, the student and the need for a guide)

304.title: The orders
304.hook: Qadiri, Naqshbandi, Chishti, Shadhili, Mevlevi and more across the world
304.howItsDone: Sufi orders, turuq, gather members around a shaykh for teaching, remembrance and service; the Qadiri, Chishti, Naqshbandi, Shadhili, Tijani and others have followers from West Africa to Southeast Asia, and many Muslims belong to no order.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the teacher and the chain, silsilah, teachers hand to hand, back through the centuries. Your line was a chain of hands. Who did you thank? Day three hundred four.

Think of a big city with one great mosque at its center. People walk to it from every direction. Some come down the wide avenue. Some take the back alleys they grew up in. Some walk slowly, some fast, some sing on the way, some go in silence. They all end up at the same door. Over the centuries, the chains of Sufi teachers grew into communities with their own names, their own practices, their own personalities, spread from Morocco to Indonesia. Each one is called by a word that means a road. Today, the roads, and five of their names.
screen: `ONE MOSQUE, MANY STREETS.` → `FROM MOROCCO TO INDONESIA.` → `EACH ONE CALLED A ROAD.`

segments.voice: The word is tariqah: a way, a road, a path. Sufis often say it like this: the shari'ah, the law, is the road everyone walks. The tariqah is the way of walking it, with a guide. And the haqiqah, the reality, is where the road leads. Now, five roads. The Qadiri order, named for 'Abd al-Qadir al-Jilani, a preacher and scholar in Baghdad who died in 1166. It's one of the oldest and most widespread, from West Africa to South Asia. The Chishti order, rooted in India through Mu'in al-Din Chishti, buried in Ajmer. Chishtis are known for open kitchens that feed anyone, and for devotional music, qawwali. The Naqshbandi order, named for Baha' al-Din Naqshband of Bukhara. Naqshbandis are known for silent remembrance of God, and a phrase: solitude in the crowd, keeping the heart with God while you're busy in the market. The Shadhili order, from Abu al-Hasan al-Shadhili, in North Africa and Egypt, which teaches its members not to leave their jobs and families, but to find the path inside ordinary life. And the Mevlevi, Rumi's order, with the turning we saw two days ago. There are many more: the Tijani across West Africa, the Rifa'i, the Suhrawardi, the Ba 'Alawi of Yemen. They differ in style, loud or quiet, music or none, withdrawing or staying in the world. Each order would say its own road is a way of following the same Prophet to the same God. Many roads in.
screen: `SHARI'AH, TARIQAH, HAQIQAH.` · `QADIRI AND CHISHTI.` · `NAQSHBANDI AND SHADHILI.` · `LOUD OR QUIET, MUSIC OR NONE.` · then, large: `MANY ROADS IN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn one order's name. Sit, and breathe. Of the five you heard, which one caught you? The Qadiri, the Chishti with its open kitchen, the Naqshbandi with its solitude in the crowd, the Shadhili in ordinary life, the Mevlevi turning. Say its name to yourself a few times, and picture its road. Later today, if you're curious, read one page about it. If you pray, you can pray for the people walking that road right now. The bell holds the time.
Tariqah. A road; a Sufi order, a way of walking the one path with a guide. Today's word.
Your line: many roads in. Today, when someone does a good thing differently from how you'd do it, notice their road before you correct them. Day three hundred four.

myth: all Sufi orders use music
they differ: loud or quiet, music or none. Naqshbandis are known for silent remembrance.
tariqah means a road or a way
the way of walking the road of the shari'ah, with a guide.
the Shadhili order teaches members to leave their jobs
it teaches them to find the path inside ordinary life.

fork.setup: you're a shopkeeper with a family, drawn to the Sufi path. which road, from today, is known for keeping the heart with God in the busy market?
options: leaving for a desert retreat for life.
the Naqshbandi way: solitude in the crowd.
giving up the shop to turn full time.
fork.reveal: solitude in the crowd: the Naqshbandi phrase for staying inwardly with God while busy in the world.

original.note: Arabic: a way, a road; a Sufi order. plural turuq.

trapdoor: what you thought: Sufi sects.
what it means: many roads, each a way of walking the same law with a guide, toward the same reality.
what a scholar hears: the triad shari'ah, tariqah, haqiqah; the Naqshbandi principle khalwat dar anjuman, solitude in the crowd.

sources.ref: the Sufi triad shari'ah, tariqah, haqiqah (classical Sufi usage)
the Naqshbandi principles of Baha' al-Din Naqshband, including khalwat dar anjuman (solitude in the crowd)

305.title: Gathered remembrance
305.hook: circles of dhikr, sung or silent
305.howItsDone: Muslims remember God with short phrases after prayer and throughout the day, often counting on the fingers or prayer beads; in Sufi orders, members also gather in circles of dhikr, aloud or silent, while some scholars object to group dhikr in unison.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the orders, tariqah: Qadiri, Chishti, Naqshbandi, Shadhili, Mevlevi, many roads to one door. Your line was many roads in. Whose road did you notice? Day three hundred five.

Picture two rooms on the same Thursday night. In the first, in a city in Morocco or Egypt, people sit shoulder to shoulder in a circle. Someone begins a phrase, and the whole room takes it up, rocking gently, the sound rising and falling like surf, for an hour. In the second, somewhere in Central Asia or Turkey, people sit in a circle too, heads bowed, eyes closed. Nobody makes a sound. You could hear a pin drop. And yet, if you asked them, both rooms are doing exactly the same thing. Today, gathered remembrance.
screen: `A ROOM THAT RISES LIKE SURF.` → `A ROOM IN TOTAL SILENCE.` → `BOTH DOING THE SAME THING.`

segments.voice: The thing is dhikr: remembrance of God, usually by repeating short phrases: la ilaha illa Allah, there is no god but God; subhan Allah, glory be to God; or simply Allah. We met dhikr earlier in the path. Every Muslim who says these after prayer is doing it. What the orders added was the circle, the halqah, remembrance done together. Some circles say it aloud, sometimes with singing and a drum. That's called jahri, out loud. Others, like the Naqshbandis, keep it silent, in the heart. That's khafi, hidden. Both point to the same verse, in Pickthall's words: "Verily in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest!" And both point to a hadith in Sahih Muslim: whenever people sit together remembering God, the angels surround them, mercy covers them, calm descends on them, and God mentions them to those who are with Him. There's another, in al-Bukhari, where God says, in a hadith qudsi: if my servant remembers Me in himself, I remember him in Myself; and if he remembers Me in a gathering, I remember him in a gathering better than that. Alone, or together. Aloud, or silent. Muslims do differ here. Some scholars object to group dhikr in unison or with music, seeing it as something later than the Prophet's practice; others defend it. We'll come to that. But the silent circle points at the heart of all of it: the tongue can say the words, but the goal is that the heart says them. The heart says it.
screen: `DHIKR — REMEMBRANCE.` · `JAHRI ALOUD, KHAFI HIDDEN.` · `IN REMEMBRANCE HEARTS FIND REST.` · `ANGELS SURROUND THE CIRCLE.` · then, large: `THE HEART SAYS IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: silent dhikr with the breath. Sit, and close your eyes if you like. Let your breath settle into its own pace. If you pray, you can say a phrase silently with each breath, not with your lips, only inside: Allah, on the breath in, and Allah, on the breath out, or la ilaha illa Allah across one breath. If you don't pray, you can use the breath alone, counting it, or simply resting on it. Let the heart do the saying. The bell holds the time.
Gathered remembrance. Circles of dhikr, sung aloud or held in silence, remembering God together. Today's word.
Your line: the heart says it. Today, in one noisy moment, a queue, a commute, a meeting, repeat one quiet word inside, and let the heart say it. Day three hundred five.

screen: `DAY 305 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE SELF TO BE TRAINED.`

original.note: Arabic: remembrance, mention; the repetition of short phrases remembering God.

trapdoor: what you thought: chanting.

306.title: The self to be trained
306.hook: the self that commands evil, that blames itself, that is at peace (12:53; 75:2; 89:27)
306.howItsDone: Muslims speak of struggling with the nafs as a lifelong part of faith, and Sufi teachers guide students through its stages, commanding, blaming and at peace, with remembrance, self-examination and service.

segments.voice: Yesterday, gathered remembrance: circles of dhikr, some rising like surf, some in total silence. Your line was the heart says it. Did one quiet word go with you through the noise? Day three hundred six.

It's eleven at night. One voice in you says: one more episode, one more slice, send the angry text, you deserve it. Ten minutes later, another voice: why did you do that? You always do that. And once in a while, on a good day, there's a third thing, not really a voice at all. A quiet. You did the right thing, or you didn't and you've made it right, and you're simply at rest. Everyone knows those three. The Qur'an names them, in three different surahs, and Sufis built a whole map of the inner life on them. Today, the self.
screen: `ONE MORE, YOU DESERVE IT.` → `WHY DID YOU DO THAT?` → `A QUIET.`

segments.voice: The Arabic word is nafs. It can mean soul, self, or ego, depending on the sentence. The first nafs is in the story of Yusuf. In Pickthall's translation: "the (human) soul enjoineth unto evil," except where God has mercy. Commentators differ on who says those words in the story, Yusuf or the wife of the man who bought him, but everyone agrees on what they describe: the self that pushes, that grabs, that wants now. It's called an-nafs al-ammarah, the self that commands. The second is in a short Meccan surah, where God swears an oath by it: "Nay, I swear by the accusing soul." An-nafs al-lawwamah, the self that blames. That's the voice at eleven-ten. Notice that God swears by it. The conscience that stings is honored, not despised. The third comes near the end of surah 89, addressed with great tenderness: "But ah! thou soul at peace!" An-nafs al-mutma'innah, the self at rest, invited to return to its Lord, content. Sufi teachers read the three as stages. The self isn't evil and isn't thrown away. It's trained, the way you'd train a strong, young horse: not broken, but taught. The work of the path is moving from commanding, through blaming, toward peace. And there's a hadith in al-Bukhari that fits: the strong one isn't the one who wins the wrestling match; the strong one is the one who controls himself when angry. Train the self.
screen: `NAFS — SOUL, SELF, EGO.` · `THE SELF THAT COMMANDS.` · `THE SELF THAT BLAMES.` · `THE SELF AT PEACE.` · then, large: `TRAIN THE SELF.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name which one spoke today. Sit, and breathe. Replay your day so far. Was there a moment the commanding self spoke, pushing for more, faster, now? A moment the blaming self spoke, stinging, maybe too harshly? And was there any moment of quiet, even a few seconds? Just name them, without judging them. Thank the blaming self for caring. If you pray, you can ask God to bring your self to peace. The bell holds the time.
Nafs. The self, in three stages in the Qur'an: commanding, blaming, and at peace. Today's word.
Your line: train the self. Today, when the commanding voice says now, answer: in ten minutes. Just once, and see who wins. Day three hundred six.

in the Qur'an, God swears by the blaming self
nay, I swear by the accusing soul.

original.note: Arabic: soul, self, ego; plural nufus or anfus.

trapdoor: what you thought: the ego is bad.
what it means: the self has stages, commanding, blaming, at peace, and the path trains it, not destroys it.
what a scholar hears: ammarah (12:53), lawwamah (75:2), mutma'innah (89:27), three Qur'anic descriptions that Sufis arranged as stages.

Sahih al-Bukhari 6114 (the strong one controls himself when angry)

307.title: Where Muslims differ
307.hook: some embrace orders and saints' shrines, others hold these as later additions, and all say keep to the Qur'an
307.howItsDone: Muslims differ on Sufi orders, visiting saints' shrines and music in worship: many embrace them, Salafi Muslims and others reject them as later additions, and many take a middle position, while all appeal to the Qur'an and the sunnah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the nafs: the self that commands, the self that blames, the self at peace. Your line was train the self. Which one spoke loudest? Day three hundred seven.

Picture two Muslim families on the same Friday. The first drives out after the prayer to a saint's tomb, a white dome with green cloth over the grave. They recite al-Fatiha for him, ask God for help near the resting place of a man they love, and give food to the poor at the gate. The second family, just as devout, would never go. They'd say, with conviction, that this isn't how the Prophet and his companions practiced, and that prayer should be directed to God alone, with nothing that looks like a go-between. For two weeks we've walked the Sufi path. Today, honestly, where Muslims differ.
screen: `A WHITE DOME, A GREEN CLOTH.` → `A FAMILY THAT WOULD NEVER GO.` → `BOTH DEVOUT.`

segments.voice: For most of Islamic history, Sufism was part of the mainstream. Great scholars of law, like al-Ghazali, were Sufis. Across the Ottoman lands, South Asia, West Africa and Southeast Asia, many ordinary Muslims belonged to an order, and visiting the shrines of saints was common. Many Muslims today still hold to that. Other Muslims have long criticized parts of it. The scholar Ibn Taymiyyah, in the fourteenth century, respected early Sufis like Junayd, but he condemned practices at graves that he believed compromised tawhid, the oneness of God. Modern Salafi movements, which aim to follow the salaf, the first generations of Muslims, hold that orders, shrine visits and musical sama' are later additions, bid'ah, and some reject tasawwuf as a separate path altogether. And many Muslims stand in between: they value tasawwuf as purifying the heart, and question some practices. Shia Muslims, for their part, visit the shrines of the Prophet's family, and their relation to the Sufi orders varies. These are real differences, and sometimes painful ones. But notice what every side says. Each argues from the Qur'an and the sunnah. The Qur'an itself tells believers, when they dispute, in Pickthall's words, to "refer it to Allah and the messenger." And a hadith in al-Bukhari says that a scholar who does his best to reach a ruling and gets it right has two rewards, and one who does his best and gets it wrong still has one. Disagreement, in Arabic ikhtilaf, is old in Islam. Underneath it, the same Book.
screen: `FOR CENTURIES, PART OF THE MAINSTREAM.` · `IBN TAYMIYYAH AND THE SALAFI CRITIQUE.` · `MANY STAND IN BETWEEN.` · `REFER IT TO ALLAH AND THE MESSENGER.` · then, large: `THE SAME QUR'AN UNDERNEATH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold two views at once, respectfully. Sit, and breathe. Picture the two families from the hook. Imagine sitting with the first at the shrine, and understanding why it moves them. Then imagine sitting with the second, and understanding why it worries them. You don't have to decide. Just hold both, with respect, for a few breaths. Then bring it closer: think of someone in your own family you disagree with, and try the same. If you pray, you can pray for both. The bell holds the time.
Where Muslims differ. On orders, shrines and music, Muslims disagree, and all of them argue from the same Qur'an. Today's word.
Your line: the same qur'an underneath. Today, in one disagreement, name out loud what you and the other person share before you name what you don't. Day three hundred seven.

match.prompt: who holds what — tap the pairs.

for most of Islamic history it was part of the mainstream; great scholars like al-Ghazali were Sufis.
Ibn Taymiyyah rejected every Sufi
he respected early Sufis like Junayd, but condemned practices at graves.
a scholar who does his best and gets it wrong still has a reward
one reward; the one who gets it right has two.

fork.setup: two devout Muslims disagree about visiting a saint's shrine. what does the Qur'an tell believers to do when they dispute?
options: refer it to Allah and the messenger.
fork.reveal: refer it to Allah and the messenger (4:59). both sides argue from the Qur'an and the sunnah.

original.note: Arabic: difference, disagreement among scholars; an old, recognized part of Islamic learning.

trapdoor: what you thought: Sufis and their critics are enemies.
what it means: devout Muslims disagree about orders, shrines and music, and all argue from the same Book and sunnah.
what a scholar hears: Ibn Taymiyyah's critique of ziyarah practices, modern Salafi reform, and the hadith of the two rewards for ijtihad (al-Bukhari 7352).

308.title: The heart's polish
308.hook: a well-known saying: everything has a polish, and the heart's polish is remembrance (Bayhaqi)
308.howItsDone: Many Muslims say SubhanAllah, alhamdulillah and Allahu akbar thirty-three or thirty-four times each after prayer or before sleep, often counting on the fingers or on prayer beads, and speak of remembrance as what keeps the heart clear.

segments.voice: Yesterday, where Muslims differ: some love the Sufi orders and the shrines, others see them as later additions, and all say keep to the Qur'an. Your line was the same Qur'an underneath. Did you manage to hold two views at once? Day three hundred eight.

Before glass mirrors, a mirror was a disc of metal: bronze, silver, polished steel. Leave one in a damp room for a season and it clouds over. Your face in it goes dim, then disappears. Nobody throws the mirror away. You take a cloth, you rub, and your face comes back. There's a well-known saying, recorded by the scholar al-Bayhaqi and attributed to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: everything has something that polishes it, and the polish of the heart is the remembrance of Allah. Scholars discuss how strong its chain of narrators is, but the picture has lasted a thousand years. Today, the last day of the Sufi path: the heart's polish.
screen: `A METAL MIRROR, CLOUDED OVER.` → `A CLOTH, AND YOUR FACE COMES BACK.` → `THE POLISH OF THE HEART.`

segments.voice: The picture starts in the Qur'an itself. Speaking of people who have hardened themselves against the truth, it says, in Pickthall's words: "Nay, but that which they have earned is rust upon their hearts." The Arabic word is ran: a film, a tarnish. A hadith in Tirmidhi explains it. When a person does wrong, a dark spot appears on the heart. If they stop, turn back and ask forgiveness, the heart is polished clean. If they keep going, the spot spreads, and that is the ran Allah mentions. So the heart isn't bad. It's a mirror that picks up dust. And the cloth is dhikr, remembrance. Another verse, in Pickthall: "Verily in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest!" This is where the teachers of the last two weeks meet. Al-Ghazali, after his crisis, wrote of the heart as a mirror that can show the truth once it's cleaned. Rumi tells a story in the Masnavi. The Chinese and the Greeks hold a painting contest. The Chinese cover their wall with color. The Greeks paint nothing at all. They polish their wall, and when the curtain between the two walls is lifted, it shines back everything the Chinese painted, and more. Rumi says the Greeks are like the Sufis, who have polished their hearts. Rabi'a's love, Junayd's sobriety, the reed flute's longing, the circles of gathered remembrance, the nafs being trained: under each of them is the same slow work with the cloth. And remember yesterday. Not every Muslim walks the Sufi orders, but remembering Allah to soften the heart is something they all share, because it comes from the Qur'an.
screen: `RUST UPON THEIR HEARTS` · `A MIRROR THAT PICKS UP DUST` · `THE CLOTH IS REMEMBRANCE` · `THE GREEKS POLISHED THEIR WALL`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a hundred remembrances, slowly. A pattern many Muslims use, which the Prophet taught his daughter Fatimah for bedtime, is SubhanAllah thirty-three times, alhamdulillah thirty-three times, Allahu akbar thirty-four. If you pray, you can say them now, softly, counting on your fingers. If you're learning, say one phrase at a time and let each one be a single pass of the cloth. Slowly matters more than finishing. If the bell comes before a hundred, you can finish afterward. The bell holds the time.
The heart's polish. The heart as a mirror that gathers dust, and remembrance, dhikr, as the cloth that brings its shine back. Today's word.

Your line: polish the heart. Today, when something leaves a film on you, a harsh word, a scroll you regret, a small unkindness of your own, stop for one breath and wipe it: one remembrance, or one honest noticing. Day three hundred eight.

fork.setup: you're a Greek painter in Rumi's contest. the Chinese are covering their wall with color. what do you do with yours?
fork.reveal: the Greeks polished until their wall shone back everything the Chinese painted. Rumi says they're like the Sufis, who polished their hearts.

original.note: Arabic: remembrance, mention. the saying calls it the polish of the heart.

trapdoor: what you thought: cleaning up your act.
what it means: the heart as a mirror that gathers the dust of wrongdoing, polished by turning back and remembering Allah.
what a scholar hears: the Qur'an's word ran in 83:14, which a hadith in Tirmidhi explains as the dark spot that spreads when a person doesn't turn back.
